I’m 65 this year, been farming these 9 mu in Quzhou for 40 years. My household has seven people — my wife, my son and his wife, their two kids, and my youngest daughter who’s still at home. My son and daughter-in-law work in a factory over in Handan, so day-to-day it’s mostly me and my wife on the land. They send some money back, but I don’t like to rely on it; a farmer ought to stand on his own feet.

We do wheat-maize double crop on all 9 mu. That’s the only system that makes sense here — wheat for flour and food security, maize for cash and feed. The wheat went in last October, same improved variety I’ve been using for six or seven years now. I know how it behaves in dry springs and wet ones. For the base fertilizer I put down farmyard manure and about 50 kg of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer per mu before sowing — that’s what I’ve done for a decade, and I’m not changing it.

Now it’s early spring and the wheat is greening up. The extension fellow says 15 kg nitrogen per mu is enough, but last year I listened to him and cut back, and my yield dropped under 400 kg/mu. So this year I’m putting about 25 kg of urea per mu down at jointing — my neighbor Lao Wang did the same and his wheat looked strong. I’ll irrigate twice more this spring: once at green-up in late March, and again at heading if the rain doesn’t come. Water from the tube well isn’t free — electricity runs about 25-30 yuan per mu each time — but dry wheat at heading is a disaster I can’t afford.

For harvest in early June, I’ll hire the combine. I can’t swing a scythe like I used to, and the window is tight. Then the real rush starts: maize has to go in within days of the wheat coming out, usually mid-June. I’ll buy hybrid seed from the agricultural supply shop — about 40 yuan per mu. I rotary-till right after wheat harvest and plant. For fertilizer, I put down 40 kg of compound and about 20 kg of urea per mu at planting, and if the leaves look yellow at the big flare stage I’ll topdress another handful. I’ll irrigate maize once or twice depending on the summer rains — July and August usually bring something, so if it’s decent, one irrigation at planting is enough. If it’s a drought year, maybe two.

For chemicals, I spray herbicide on both crops. If I see aphids on the wheat or armyworm on the maize, I’ll spray insecticide, but I don’t just spray for nothing — every bottle is cash out of my pocket.

Labor is tight. My wife and I handle the spreading, irrigating, and watching, but during wheat harvest and maize planting that one-week window, I’ll hire maybe 4-5 days of help from the village lads. Hired labor is 120 yuan a day now, so I keep it to a minimum.

I expect about 430 kg per mu for wheat and around 480 kg per mu for maize if the weather holds. Total input costs — seed, fertilizer, water, chemicals, hired help — will run about 4,800 yuan. That’s a lot of cash to lay out when you’re living on last year’s grain, but skimping on fertilizer is false economy. I’d rather tighten our belt at home than risk a bad yield.
